premises.name: Save Changes to untitled?
premises.logline: The universe is an unsaved 16-colour Paint file with exactly one palette slot left. When the Hand finally clicks Save, whichever colour covers more of the canvas gets the slot and exists forever, and the other is dithered down to grey.
premises.world: Creation is untitled.bmp, 640x480. It has been open since 1998 and has never been saved. Fourteen greys and a black came free with the palette. One slot was taken long ago, so 'SUN (YELLOW IS TAKEN)' is not a joke here. It is the first article of the constitution. One slot is left. Above the canvas is the Hand, which has two buttons, so creation has two churches. The Left Click serves Colour 1, the Right Click serves Colour 2, and each is sure the other was made with the wrong finger. The faint grey doodles in the backdrop are earlier drafts, too pale to fight and still hoping. The cursor sometimes drifts across the sky, and nobody looks at it directly.
premises.who_you_play: The drawings. They look exactly like the art because they are the art. The Hand can only draw one kind of person: a box, two dots, a line, and a flat stroke on top that is just how the Hand draws hair. The overalls are the only part the Hand ever filled in, so they are the only place a candidate colour is allowed to live.
premises.why_paint: A 16-colour file can only keep one more colour, so saving forces a vote. The free slot goes to whichever candidate is most present on the canvas, and every pixel of the loser is converted to the nearest grey. A painted pixel is a vote and a painted pixel is survival. Nobody knows the score during the match because a picture does not add itself up while it is still being drawn. The reveal is the Save. The match freezes, a hand-drawn 'Save changes to untitled?' box appears and the Hand clicks Yes. A progress bar crawls while the pixels are tallied, then the loser's colour dithers to grey one row at a time.
premises.teams: Colour 1 against Colour 2. The Edit Colors dialog only ever offers its candidates in pairs, and the Hand never decides between them. That is why the pairs are authored and why the draw is random. On the pre-match screen, two squares in the palette strip light up. The win never lasts, because the program forgets the palette when it closes. That explains the rematch: the election runs again every time.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = the Airbrush, a holy relic, and its speckle is a known flaw. Roller = the Brush at its widest square tip, dragged. Bucket = Fill With Color, the most feared tool in creation, which leaks through any gap in a line. Mister = the Airbrush on its smallest nozzle, called 'a rumour of colour'. Later: the Line tool fired at 45 degrees, the Eraser (it paints white, which here means deletion), Pick Colour (steals a pixel's allegiance) and the Text tool (types an insult that is also a platform).
arenas: Close Quarters: The Corner. The bottom-left 100x100 pixels, where the Hand always starts drawing and then gives up.
King of the Hill: Curve Tool Hill. Its summit is the one spot the Hand looks at most.
Turbulence: Mid-Undo. Platforms flicker between versions of history while someone holds Ctrl+Z.
Movement Course: Warm-Up Scribbles. Lines the Hand drew to test the mouse, ridden like rails.
The Selection: a marching-ants rectangle being dragged across the canvas, and everything inside it goes along.
Magnifier: the same arena at 800%, which counts as heresy because you can see the pixels.
premises.tone: Deadpan scripture from inside software that does not care. The drawings are serene about being drawings and terrified of 'Don't Save'. Captions: 'CTRL+Z (DO NOT SAY IT ALOUD)' / 'SLOT 16: VACANT SINCE 1998' / on the results screen, 'PALETTE UPDATED. (UNTIL YOU CLOSE THE PROGRAM.)'
premises.art_fit: The closest fit possible: here the crude art is physics. Aliasing, leaky fills, marching ants and the 'platform|' text box are natural phenomena. The world is grey because the palette had no room for anything else, which explains outright why team hues never appear in the world. 'by matt (age 7)' becomes the signature of God.
premises.risks: It is meta and could become a one-joke premise unless the theology keeps escalating. It sits so close to the art direction that it adds a reason more than a new world. Paint and Windows chrome must be evoked in the author's own crude drawing, never traced: no logos and no real dialogs. Windows-98 nostalgia may read as a period piece to younger players.

coherence.reason: Here the art direction is the physics: one free palette slot explains the grey world, the missing team hues, the Paint tools as weapons and the Save dialog as the reveal, though the authored pairs only half-explain the random draw and it risks being one joke unless the two-button theology keeps escalating.

identity.reason: The tightest fit in the set: the crude art becomes the physics, the empty palette slot explains why team hues never appear in the world, the Save dialog is a cheap and unforgettable end-of-match reveal, and the pitch fits in one line ('two colours fight for the last palette slot before the file is saved'), though it has to keep escalating to avoid being one joke and Windows chrome has to be drawn generically.

production.reason: The fiction is the art direction itself: the 16-colour palette explains the grey world, the Save dialog is a perfect cheap reveal, Left Click versus Right Click gives the teams a theology, and the forgotten palette justifies endless rematches.

premises.name: Kerb Appeal
premises.logline: After people moved out, houses became the dominant species: proud, petty and obsessed with what the neighbours think. The covenant says the whole street must be one colour, and every square metre painted is a vote.
premises.world: The buildings woke up when the people left and kept every one of their habits. They hold residents' association meetings, measure hedges and leave passive-aggressive notes. The Meadowbrook covenant says the whole estate must be one colour, voted on each year by surface area, not by household. So polling day is a full-contact paint war between the two ends of the cul-de-sac. Bare grey render is shameful, and it is all anyone is allowed until the vote.
premises.who_you_play: Houselings, the children of houses. The box head is a house: the dot eyes are the upstairs windows, the flat mouth is the letterbox and the flat cap is the roof extension that never got planning permission. The overalls are scaffolding and dust sheets, worn while the family is 'having work done'. The reveal that the art has been houses all along costs nothing to draw. Damage is cracks, and a respawn is 'underpinning'.
premises.why_paint: Paint is a house's clothing, reputation and vote. The colour that covers more of the street becomes compulsory for every house for a year, and the losing end has to live in it. The covenant forbids canvassing or tallying while voting is open. The reveal is Dust Sheets Off: all the work is done under sheets, the sheets come off at the AGM, the Chair reads the count from the minutes, and somebody gasps.
premises.teams: The Odds against the Evens, the two sides of the street. Colours are random because the covenant's approved swatch card permits only certain 'heritage pairs', and this year's pair is drawn from the Chair's mug. Every other colour is a breach of covenant, which is why team hues never appear in the scenery.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = the Pebbledash Gun. Roller = the Long-Handled Roller ('Dad's roller, do not lose it'). Bucket = the Neighbour's Bucket, borrowed in 2009 and never returned. Mister = the Hosepipe on Mist, in breach of the hosepipe ban. Later: the Pressure Washer (strips enemy paint, deeply passive-aggressive) and the Gnome (thrown, does nothing, very offensive).
arenas: Close Quarters: The Shared Driveway. Who owns the middle strip is a matter for solicitors.
King of the Hill: The Detached. One rich house on a three-foot hill that everyone resents.
Turbulence: Bin Day. Wheelie bins blowing about as moving platforms.
Movement Course: The Show Home. Every surface perfectly level, which the houselings find deeply suspicious.
The Community Hall: stacking chairs and a tea urn, on the night of the AGM itself.
The New Build: half-finished, all scaffolding, with a sign promising 'LUXURY'.
premises.tone: Net-curtain passive aggression reported like war news, with an estate-agent deadpan. Captions: 'CHARMING 1-BED SLAB. NEEDS WORK.' / 'NUMBER 4 HAS PAINTED HIS GUTTERING. WE ARE ALL VERY UPSET.' / on the results screen, 'Kerb appeal: ACHIEVED. House price: up 3%.'
premises.art_fit: It reinterprets the box-head figure without redrawing a pixel. Rectangle-tool houses are what Paint does best and everyone draws houses this way. 'Interim Approved Grey' explains why team hues are absent until the vote, and grey slabs are unpainted render.
premises.risks: The British suburban register may not travel. Readers from the US will hear 'HOA', which helps. The houses-are-people idea needs one clear on-screen tell, such as a chimney on a houseling's cap, or players will read the figures as ordinary painters. Planning satire can tip from charming into smug.

coherence.reason: The most Splatoon-like move in the set: a confident new dominant species whose bodies, the box head as a house with window eyes and letterbox mouth, are the existing art; voting by surface area and Dust Sheets Off explain territory and the reveal cleanly, though the British suburban register may not travel.

identity.reason: Houses as the dominant species reinterprets the box head for free (windows for eyes, a letterbox mouth, the cap as a roof extension) and is truly Splatoon-weird, but the British cul-de-sac register may not travel and the 'houses are people' idea needs a clear visual tell.

production.reason: Reinterpreting the box head as a house (windows for eyes, letterbox mouth, roof cap) with no redraw is a brilliant species-level weirdness, and covenant vote by surface area explains coverage perfectly, though the register is very British.

premises.name: The Last Coat
premises.logline: The universe is ending on schedule, and before the next one starts somebody has to choose its base coat. The departing cosmos has hired two crews of decorators and is letting the job decide.
premises.world: Far future, after heat death. Every star is out and every galaxy has gone grey and settled. Creation is renewed the way a room is, with a fresh base coat over the old, and the colour of that coat becomes the next universe's starting conditions: its physics, its sky, its gods. The Cosmos is very tired and has hired contractors. Each match is the last job in existence, and then, being a universe, it happens again.
premises.who_you_play: The Decorators of the End, a guild of tradesmen older than matter. They have painted every universe there has ever been and remember none of them, because a fresh coat always takes the memory with it. The flat cap and overalls are the uniform. The box head is the shape that survives a universe reset most cheaply, which makes it the most efficient head in existence.
premises.why_paint: Paint is the next universe's undercoat. Every painted surface becomes physical law next time, so coverage decides what the next cosmos is made of. Nobody can score until the coat is dry. The reveal is the Big Bang: a white flash, then the next universe's first sky fades in, in the winning colour, with a caption like 'UNIVERSE #4,118,002: mostly orange'. Rematches are simply the next universe.
premises.teams: Two crews from the same guild, one job and two quotes. Colours are random because the Cosmos signed off on several swatch cards and forgot which, so each match draws from the approved shortlist. A caption: 'previous universe: blue (complaints received)'.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = the Nebula Gun, sprayer tech from a dead galactic civilisation. Roller = the Event Horizon, which flattens everything it touches. Bucket = the Supernova: one tin, all at once, very bright. Mister = Background Radiation: a faint fine haze, everywhere, eventually.
arenas: Close Quarters: A Pocket Dimension, a cupboard of the multiverse.
King of the Hill: The Last Mountain, the final high ground before matter gives up.
Turbulence: The Expansion. The arena stretches apart as space thins out.
Movement Course: The Asteroid Belt. Rocks drifting into position for no stated reason.
The Old Coats: a grey ruin of previous universes, where peeling layers reveal past winners.
Planck Length: the smallest possible arena, two jumps wide.
premises.tone: Epic cosmic scale delivered as shrugging trade talk. The end of everything is a Tuesday job with a quote attached. Captions: 'heat death (on schedule, no extras)' / 'last star: do not move, do not paint, client is sentimental' / 'GOD (subcontractor)'.
premises.art_fit: It keeps the painter figure intact while making the scale cosmic. The white canvas is the void between universes, grey slabs are the last settled matter, and light-grey doodles are dead galaxies. Crude drawing is the guild's house style, kept because nobody survives long enough to learn a better one.
premises.risks: Tiny 2D arenas and cosmic scale need the captions to bridge the gap. Its humour overlaps The Final Inspection and The Decorated Dead (eternal tradesmen, an absent client), so expect to pick one. The Big Bang reveal needs a cheap but strong visual: a flash and a one-colour fill will do.

coherence.reason: It keeps the tradesmen and makes them cosmic: coverage becomes the next universe's undercoat, the Big Bang reveal is cheap and spectacular, rematches are simply the next universe, and 'mostly orange' is a perfect caption, though the swatch-card reason for random pairs is weak.

identity.reason: It is a great one-line hook ('decorators choose the base coat of the next universe') that keeps the painter figure intact, and the 'UNIVERSE #4,118,002: mostly orange' rematch joke is excellent, but the cosmic scale has to be carried by captions in small 2D arenas.

production.reason: Cosmic stakes delivered as trade talk is a confident tone, and 'UNIVERSE #4,118,002: mostly orange' plus rematch-as-next-universe is a superb cheap loop; the gap between tiny arenas and cosmic scale is the main weakness.

premises.name: Feed the Hues
premises.logline: Every colour is a god, and a god exists only while something in the world is its colour. Since the Fading the gods are starving, and at each festival two of them, sworn enemies across the colour wheel, are fed by their congregations in ritual combat.
premises.world: The world was once so colourful that the gods were fat and lazy. Then came the Fading, when everything bleached grey and the gods began to waste away, because a hue nobody sees stops existing. The authored pairs (blue and orange, pink and green, blue and yellow) sit nearly opposite each other on the wheel, so every pairing is an ancient blood feud. Yellow is the richest god because it owns the sun outright, and everyone resents it.
premises.who_you_play: Acolytes. The flat cap is a mitre flattened by centuries of humility. The box head is required by the First Commandment, THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL, because a good likeness of a face would steal attention from the gods. So every faithful self-portrait is a square, two dots and a line. Overalls are vestments in the god's colour.
premises.why_paint: Paint is food: worship made visible. Every painted surface is a mouthful the god can see, a god feeds on area, and the god that eats more survives the season. The score is hidden because no mortal may know a god's appetite. The reveal: one enormous crude eye opens over the arena, the god slurps up its colour, and the result is shown by which god looks fuller.
premises.teams: Two congregations of mercenary believers, devout for exactly three minutes. The gods once fought over who got to compete, so now the Wheel decides: it spins before each match and the faithful serve whichever pair it lands on.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = the Censer, swung on a chain, spraying holy paint. Roller = the Prayer Wheel, rolled along floors, blessing every surface it touches. Bucket = the Offering Bowl, emptied in one devout splash. Mister = the Aspergillum, the holy-water sprinkler, which the elderly prefer.
arenas: Close Quarters: The Confessional. Two people in a box and a lot of feelings.
King of the Hill: The High Altar, the slab the god looks at first.
Turbulence: The Breath of the Wind God, who is not a contestant and will not stop interfering.
Movement Course: The Pilgrim's Path, a route of ritual jumps nobody can explain.
The Grey Chapel: a temple to the dead god Taupe, now neutral ground.
The Wheel: a slowly rotating arena, the lottery itself.
premises.tone: Solemn liturgy about absurd, petty gods, like an illuminated manuscript drawn by an eight-year-old. Captions: 'SUN (property of YELLOW. no.)' / 'statue of PINK (it's a blob. that's the point)' / 'here lies TAUPE. nobody noticed for 200 years'.
premises.art_fit: Very strong, because crude art becomes religious law. Drawing badly is piety and a polished asset would be blasphemy, which gives the author a permanent excuse and a running joke. Team hues never appear in the world because a god's colour is holy, and grey slabs are the Faded world the gods lost.
premises.risks: The religious satire must stay about invented, silly gods and never touch real faiths. Starving gods could darken the tone if the eating reveal turns grotesque rather than comic. The complementary-pair lore constrains future pairs (blue/yellow is only roughly opposite, so the lore should say 'enemies' rather than claim exact opposites).

coherence.reason: Gods that feed on visible area make coverage the whole point, the hidden score is divine appetite, and THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL turns the crude art into piety for good; its weakness is that the Wheel is a thin reason for the colour pairs, and the starving and religious angles need care.

identity.reason: 'THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL' is the best justification in the set for the crude art, and starving colour gods explain why coverage is the score, but religious satire carries storefront risk and the complementary-pair lore constrains future colour pairs.

production.reason: 'THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL' turns crude art into piety permanently, and petty colour gods (dead Taupe, greedy Yellow) generate jokes without end, but religious satire needs care and the eating reveal must stay comic.

premises.name: Hue Season
premises.logline: Wild colour went extinct centuries ago. The last colour lives in flocks kept by flat-capped Hueherds, and in Hue Season two flocks are let out to nest: whichever flock nests on the most ground breeds next year's colour.
premises.world: Colour is an animal. It once roosted on everything, until the Great Fading hunted, bleached and paved it into extinction, which is why the world is light grey, dark grey and outlined black. The only living colour survives in domesticated flocks: a liquid, murmuring substance kept in pails by an old rural guild. In Hue Season, two flocks are released on neutral ground. Colour nests on surfaces, and where it nests, it breeds.
premises.who_you_play: Hueherds: box-headed, flat-capped rural keepers, like shepherds or beekeepers. Their overalls are coloured because they are covered in the flock, the way a beekeeper wears bees. The box head is the traditional herding hood, worn so the colour does not nest on your face. They are the painter tradesman shifted one step into the weird.
premises.why_paint: Paint is a living flock and every painted patch is a nest. Coverage is breeding ground, and the herd with the most nests leaves with the most colour for next year, in a world where colour is the whole economy. The score is hidden because colour roosts at dusk: during play it is restless and shifting, with twitching edges, and it only settles when the light goes. The reveal is the Roost Count: the guild elder walks the field at sunset counting nests, and settled paint stops twitching patch by patch.
premises.teams: The flocks migrate, so each season the Guild draws lots from the breeding ledger to decide which two surviving breeds meet: blue against orange this year, pink against green the next. Team hues never appear in the world because wild colour is extinct. Any colour you see belongs to somebody.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = the Scatterhorn, which startles a flock into a fast spray. Roller = the Drover, a broad drum that herds colour flat along the ground. Bucket = the Release: a full pail opened, so a whole flock pours out and nests at once. Mister = the Smoker, borrowed from beekeeping, which calms the flock into a drifting haze that settles slowly. Later: the Whistle (calls nearby colour to you) and the Lure.
arenas: Close Quarters: The Coop. A cramped roosting shed: 'MIND THE SPILLS (THEY ARE ALIVE)'.
King of the Hill: Old Tor. The last wild colour was seen here, and a plaque reads 'LAST WILD YELLOW, 1712. (YELLOW IS TAKEN.)'
Turbulence: The Moor. Wind scatters flocks, and Hueherds hate it.
Movement Course: The Training Paddock, where young herders learn to keep up.
The Bleachery: a ruined factory from the Great Fading, still a bit sinister.
Show Field: a county fair with prize rosettes and a cake nobody is allowed to paint.
premises.tone: A deadpan nature documentary crossed with a country fair, with quiet melancholy about a grey world and agricultural pedantry played straight. Captions: 'ORANGE (MIGRATORY). DO NOT FEED AFTER MIDNIGHT.' / 'GREY: NATIVE. COMMON. UNLOVED.' / on the loss screen, 'Your flock has gone quiet. It will be fine. Probably.'
premises.art_fit: It explains the art's rules outright. The world is grey because colour is extinct, and team hues never appear in it because colour is livestock. Leaky bucket fills are flocks spilling, and wobbly lines suit a rustic world.
premises.risks: 'Colour is an animal' has to be shown, not told: twitching paint edges and a murmuring sound are needed, or it reads as ordinary paint with lore attached. The extinction backstory must not be overplayed against the slapstick. It shares 'living colour' with Feed the Hues and Two Colours Out of Space.

coherence.reason: Colour as near-extinct livestock explains the grey world and the colour-free scenery, the Roost Count at dusk is a lovely reason the score is hidden, and the Hueherds are a step into the weird from the tradesmen, but it only works if the paint visibly lives, which costs art time.

identity.reason: This is the closest analogue to Splatoon's species logic without copying it: colour is extinct livestock, so the grey world and the absent team hues are ecology, and flat-capped Hueherds are an ownable, pitchable figure, though the paint needs some living animation (twitching edges, a murmuring sound) or the idea reads as lore stuck on ordinary paint.

production.reason: Colour as extinct livestock is truly weird, explains the grey world and the absent hues outright, and Hueherds keep the cap, but the twitching, living paint needs animation and sound to sell it.

premises.name: Swatch
premises.logline: In a hardware superstore closed for a century, the paint-chip cards came alive and built a religion: one day the Customer will return and choose the Colour of the Year, and the whole store had better be wearing it.
premises.world: Aisle 14, Decorating, is a nation of paint-chip people, each citizen named after its shade: Burnt Mandarin, Hushed Teal, Seaside Promise, Mushroom Whisper. The lights hum and dust drifts. The swatches have divided the aisles into territories and keep the old rites: the annual Swatch-Off and the Colour of the Year. They believe the shutters will rise again. Grey slabs are unpainted shelving, and the backdrop is stock nobody wanted.
premises.who_you_play: Swatchfolk. The box head is a paint-chip card, a square with a colour name on the back. Their flat caps and overalls come from the staff room, copied from the store mascot on a faded poster, 'the Paint Man' (designed 1961, never updated), because staff uniforms are holy. Every player has a ridiculous shade name on their HUD.
premises.why_paint: A swatch is its colour, and every surface wearing your shade is a vote for your shade. When the Customer returns, they will choose whatever colour the store already seems to be, and that shade will be in every home in the world. The losing shade is moved to the Discontinued shelf. Each match is a rehearsal for the Return, so nobody counts until it comes. The reveal: the shutters rattle, a silhouette appears in the doorway (it is a mannequin), the tannoy crackles 'And the Colour of the Year is...' and the store lights come on aisle by aisle.
premises.teams: Before each match, the swatch fan is spun and two shades are drawn: the Ritual of the Fan. That explains the random authored pairs directly: blue/orange is 'Lagoon Sigh vs Tangerine Opinion'. Team hues never appear in the scenery because a shade that is not in play is still in its card, waiting.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = the Tester Pot Spray. Roller = the Display Roller, still with its price tag. Bucket = the Mixing Tin, fresh from the tinting machine. Mister = the Shaker's mist, which hangs in the air. Later: the Price Gun (stickers enemies, slowing them) and the Trolley (a weapon and a vehicle).
arenas: Close Quarters: The Tinting Booth.
King of the Hill: The Display Pyramid. A tower of stacked tins: 'DO NOT TAKE FROM THE BOTTOM'.
Turbulence: The Loading Bay. Shutter doors open and close, and the wind comes through.
Movement Course: The Garden Centre, overgrown and wild.
Customer Services: a bell nobody answers.
The Discontinued Range: a sealed back room of losing shades.
premises.tone: Cargo-cult corporate devotion in a deadpan retail voice. The swatches revere signage. Captions: 'MUSHROOM WHISPER (WE DO NOT TALK ABOUT MUSHROOM WHISPER)' / 'IN STORE ONLY. FOREVER.' / on the results screen, 'The Customer has chosen: BURNT MANDARIN. Clean up on aisle everything.'
premises.art_fit: Square paint chips make the box head natural, shelving makes clean grey slabs, and absurd shade names are cheap, short jokes. It keeps the tradesman uniform while making its wearers weirder. Crude drawing reads as cheap hand-made shop signage.
premises.risks: Shade names and brands must be invented, never parodies of real paint companies or their shade names. Without the cult element it collapses into a generic shop. The Customer reveal needs variation so it is not the same gag every match. It overlaps Hue Season (colour as identity).

coherence.reason: A paint chip makes the box head obvious, the Ritual of the Fan is a direct reason for random pairs, and absurd shade names are an endless supply of cheap jokes, but the Customer reveal could grow stale.

identity.reason: Paint-chip people with absurd shade names on the HUD are a highly marketable, cheap joke engine, and the square chip fits the box head, but it leans on the cult element and must avoid parodying real paint brands.

production.reason: Absurd shade names are an endless, cheap joke supply (Tangerine Opinion versus Lagoon Sigh), paint-chip squares justify the box head, and the cargo-cult Customer reveal fits, though without the cult it becomes a generic shop.

premises.name: Set As Desktop Background
premises.logline: On the family PC, one picture a week is Set As Desktop Background, which makes the desktop the house's fridge door, and Mum judges by one rule: 'ooh, lots of colour!'. The drawings are Dad's decorating crew, drawn twice by two siblings, and they know where losing pictures go.
premises.world: A beige family computer in a back bedroom, around 1999. Two siblings have each drawn 'MY DAD AT WORK' into the same untitled file. The desktop is the only gallery that matters, because it is seen every time the computer turns on, for a whole week. Losing pictures go in the Recycle Bin, and the Bin is emptied on Sundays. The drawings know all of this and have built their whole culture around it. The cursor crosses the sky like weather.
premises.who_you_play: Dad, as a seven-year-old draws him with the Rectangle and Line tools: a box head, two dots, a flat mouth, Dad's flat cap and Dad's overalls, which got the first Fill Bucket click. Every figure believes he is the real Dad. The painter tradesman survives as the subject of the picture, seen through a child.
premises.why_paint: Grown-ups do not judge art by subject or skill. They judge it by how much colour is on it, and white paper reads as 'not finished'. So coverage is the only criterion of the only authority this world has. Nobody can judge a picture while standing inside it, so there is no running score. The reveal is Mum arriving. The cursor glides in, the camera pulls back to the whole canvas and a 'Set As Desktop Background' bar fills slowly. Then the desktop appears with the winning half behind the icons, while the losing half is dragged to the Bin.
premises.teams: BIG and LITTLE, the two siblings. Colours are random because whoever reaches the palette first gets the swatch, and the authored pairs are the swatches that got clicked this week. A caption owns up to it: 'pink was not a choice. pink was an accident.'
premises.weapons: Dad's kit as the kid drew it. Sprayer = Dad's spray gun, drawn as a hairdryer because that is what Matt thinks it is. Roller = Dad's roller, drawn far too big. Bucket = the tin, which in a drawing just tips everything out at once and leaks through any gap in the lines. Mister = the plant mister from the windowsill, which Matt insists counts. Later: the Rubber (erases to white) and Glitter (wins tie-breaks, because grown-ups love glitter).
arenas: Close Quarters: 'OUR HOUSE'. Every room is drawn the same size, the loo included.
King of the Hill: 'DAD ON A LADDER'. The ladder is far taller than the house.
Turbulence: 'A STORM (SCARY)'. The clouds have faces and are angry about it.
Movement Course: 'THE OBSTICAL COURSE AT SCHOOL', spelt the way Matt spelt it.
The Recycle Bin: a dark arena of losing pictures, where respawns are bitter.
The Clipboard: the picture got pasted in twice, so the arena overlaps itself.
premises.tone: Affectionate and deadpan, with a child's spelling and total authority, and slightly bleak about the Bin. Captions: 'THIS IS THE SUN. IT IS NOT YELLOW BECAUSE YELLOW IS TAKEN' / 'DO NOT MOVE THIS CLOUD (IT IS STUCK ON)' / on the results screen, 'VERY GOOD. (did not look)'.
premises.art_fit: Excellent. 'by matt (age 7)' is no longer a gag but the world's author credit, and every mistake is lore. Backdrop doodles are the rest of each sibling's drawing (the house, the dog, a sun). The Paint toolbar and palette strip can frame the HUD.
premises.risks: It is near the 'it's all a kid's drawing' cliché, so it lives or dies on the 'lots of colour' rule and the Bin. It overlaps Save Changes (same file, same canvas), so the author would pick one of the two. Mum and Dad must stay offscreen, as a cursor and a voice. Paint chrome must be drawn generically. Keep the Bin funny, not sad.

coherence.reason: 'Ooh, lots of colour!' is a perfect, human explanation of coverage-only judging, and it keeps Dad the decorator and makes 'by matt (age 7)' canon, but 'it's a kid's drawing' is less weird than the brief wants.

identity.reason: It makes 'by matt (age 7)' the canon author credit, keeps the tradesman figure as Dad seen through a child, has a universal and warm rule ('ooh, lots of colour!') that explains why coverage is the score, and the wallpaper reveal is very marketable, but it is near the 'it's all a kid's drawing' cliché.

production.reason: 'Ooh, lots of colour' is a clever reason to judge by coverage and Dad keeps the tradesman, but it sits close to the it's-all-a-kid's-drawing cliché and is less weird than the brief wants.

premises.name: Planning Permission
premises.logline: You are the little people architects draw into plans for scale. The council builds exactly what is coloured in when the committee presses Print, and two rival developers have sent you into the same drawing.
premises.world: Every building in town starts as a drawing submitted to the planning office, which still runs on one 1998 PC with nothing installed but Paint. Whatever is coloured in at Print is legally what gets built, and by whom. Each plan is inhabited by its scale figures, the stick people drawn in to show how big a door is. They have learned to hold a brush, and they work for whichever developer pasted them in.
premises.who_you_play: Scale figures. The box head is there because they were drawn with the Rectangle tool. The flat cap is there because the council's template figure was drawn in 1998 by a planning officer called Derek, who wore one, and every figure since has been copy-pasted from Derek. Overalls are in the developer's colour, as the legend requires.
premises.why_paint: Coloured area is approved build area. Paint a slab in your developer's colour and your developer builds there. Nobody can count until the drawing is printed, because the printout is the only legal copy. The reveal is the committee pressing Print: the office dot-matrix printer chatters the drawing out line by line, and the tally sweeps down the screen with it. The last line printed carries a rubber stamp.
premises.teams: Two developers, for example 'Greybrook Homes' against 'Matt Construction (Est. age 7)'. Colours are random because the council's drawing legend is reissued every session from Schedule 4, 'Approved Hatching Colours', by drawing lots, to prevent favouritism. Every other colour is reserved for listed buildings, which is why team hues never appear in the scenery.
premises.weapons: These are Paint's own tools, issued by the council. Sprayer = the Airbrush. Roller = the Brush at its widest. Bucket = the Fill tool, which leaks through any gap in a boundary line, the cause of every planning dispute in history. Mister = 'Airbrush (Smallest Setting)', for landscaping. Later: the Eraser ('Demolition Order') and the Rectangle ('Proposed Extension', which places cover).
arenas: Close Quarters: 'Application 04/117: Garden Shed'.
King of the Hill: 'Application 98/001: Hill (Retrospective)'.
Turbulence: 'Proposed Wind Farm'. The turbines are already running in the drawing.
Movement Course: 'Fire Escape Compliance Diagram'.
Untitled.bmp: an application saved without a name, now legally binding.
The Marching Ants: a selection box that is about to be cut and pasted into another parish.
premises.tone: Planning-office deadpan, dry and municipal and very slightly sinister. Captions: 'PROPOSED CLOUD (DO NOT MOVE)' / 'SCALE 1:WHAT' / on the results screen, 'SUBMITTED BY: matt (age 7). STATUS: APPROVED'.
premises.art_fit: Very strong. The crude art is literally the planning document, so every crudeness is explained: of course it looks like this, the council drew it. Eraser blocks, the selection box and the 'platform|' text box become planning amendments. Grey slabs are unapproved land.
premises.risks: It shares the 'world is a Paint file' frame with Save Changes and Set As Desktop Background, so the author would choose one. The painter-tradesman side is thin, since the figures are decorators only by job description. The dot-matrix reveal needs sound and animation work to sell it. Municipal humour is dry and may land unevenly.

coherence.reason: Coloured area as approved build area and Derek's copy-pasted cap explain the mechanics and the figure well, but it is dry municipal satire and overlaps the other Paint-file premises.

identity.reason: Scale figures copy-pasted from Derek's 1998 template is a clever explanation of the figure, but municipal dryness is hard to sell on a Steam page and it overlaps the other 'world is a Paint file' premises.

production.reason: Coloured area as approved build area is a tight mechanic and Derek's copy-pasted template figure is inspired, but the municipal dryness and the dot-matrix reveal limit its range and its fun.

premises.name: Inside the Lines
premises.logline: The people in a budget colouring book are born as empty outlines and become real only once they are coloured in. Two kids are colouring the same book from opposite ends, and the outline people have picked sides.
premises.world: A colouring book is a country of outlines, printed slightly off-register on cheap paper. Everything starts as black line on white, and white means unfinished, almost not there. A thing that gets coloured becomes solid and permanent. The national commandment, printed at the top of every page, is STAY INSIDE THE LINES. Scripture is made of printed instructions ('colour the ball red!'). Heresy is going outside the lines, which the Bucket does constantly.
premises.who_you_play: Outline people from page 12, 'The Decorator', so the flat cap and overalls are the book's own picture and the tradesman theme is the template. Your overalls are coloured because kids always colour the clothes first, and that is what made you real enough to fight. Your face stays uncoloured, because it is printed: two dots and a line. A big paint-by-numbers digit is printed on your back like a football shirt.
premises.why_paint: Colour is existence. Uncoloured floor is barely real, and at the end of the match it simply is not there. The war is to finish the page in your colour before the book is closed. Nobody counts during the match, because the book's own rule is that you check your work when you are done. The reveal is the page held up to a grown-up, with the back-cover scoring chart filling in: 'HOW MUCH DID YOU COLOUR?' and a printed gold star for one side.
premises.teams: FRONT and BACK, the two ends of the book, which will meet in the middle. Colours are random because the book came with one four-pencil pack and the kids swap pencils on every page. The authored pairs are the sets printed on the packet ('blue & orange set').
premises.weapons: Sprayer = a pencil scribbled fast and scratchy. Roller = the side of a chunky triangle pencil. Bucket = a paintbrush with far too much water, which the book specifically tells you not to use. Mister = a water-brush pen. Later: the Sharpener (fires shavings), the Ruler (draws a straight line that becomes a platform), and the forbidden Black Pencil, used only to 'fix the lines'.
arenas: Close Quarters: a maze page ('help the dog find his bone!').
King of the Hill: a printed hill with 'colour the hill GREEN' on it, an instruction everyone ignores.
Turbulence: a windy-day page full of printed kites and swirls.
Movement Course: the 'learn to colour' practice page, with labelled shapes.
Spot The Difference: two near-identical half-arenas side by side.
The Middle Pages: where the two ends of the book finally meet.
premises.tone: Mock-scriptural and pious about something childish, sincere to the last line. Captions: 'STAY INSIDE THE LINES (this is the law)' / 'colour the sky BLUE (blue is in use, sorry)' / 'page 12 of 48. Ages 4+'.
premises.art_fit: Strong. Black outlines over white are the printed book, and the colour players add is the only colour in the world, which is the no-team-hues rule exactly. The leaky bucket becomes heresy, played for comedy. Light-grey backdrop doodles are the pictures from the next page showing through. Off-register printing explains the wobbly lines.
premises.risks: Printed outlines are crisper than mouse-wobble Paint lines, so the book has to be visibly cheap. 'Colour is existence' overlaps Save Changes; this is the paper-and-childhood version. The theology joke needs restraint. The paint-by-numbers digits could clutter split-screen views if they are drawn large.

coherence.reason: Colour-is-existence and the decorator on page 12 are strong, but crisp printed outlines on paper fight the Paint.exe look, and it is the paper version of Save Changes.

identity.reason: 'Colour is existence' plus the book's own decorator page is a clean explanation for both the figure and the mechanic, but printed outlines fight the mouse-wobble aesthetic, and it is a paper version of Save Changes.

production.reason: Colour as existence and the page-12 Decorator template are strong and on-brand, but printed outlines fight the mouse-wobble look and it overlaps Save Changes in a weaker form.

premises.name: The Cave Wall
premises.logline: Forty thousand years ago, the first people learned that whoever paints the cave wall is remembered and whoever doesn't is forgotten. So they fought for it with spat pigment and mammoth-fat rollers, and the score is read out by an archaeologist's torch forty millennia late.
premises.world: The Palaeolithic as it really was: a constant, vicious contest for wall space, because history only remembers whoever is on the wall when the cave entrance collapses. There are two timelines. The matches happen in the deep past, and every result is announced in the far future by a nervous academic with a torch. Every arena caption is that academic's interpretation, and the academic is always confidently wrong.
premises.who_you_play: The first people, drawn the way they drew themselves, because box heads are simply the cave-painting style. The archaeologists label the flat cap 'hat (ceremonial, purpose unknown)' and the overalls 'fur garment (dyed, anachronistically)'.
premises.why_paint: Paint is memory. With no writing, a painted wall is the only proof you existed, and coverage is how much of history is about you. Nobody alive ever learns the result, because the match is only scored in the future. That is why there is no running score. The reveal: the arena goes dark, a torch beam sweeps slowly across the wall, the archaeologist gasps, and a museum placard names the winning band.
premises.teams: Two rival bands. Colours are random because pigment depends on whichever berries, clays and minerals are in season, and the authored pairs are this season's harvest. The anachronism is admitted: 'BLUE (should not exist for 30,000 years. sorry)'.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = mouth-blown pigment, the real technique behind ancient hand stencils, weaponised. Roller = a log rolled in pigmented fat. Bucket = the Skull Bowl, catalogued as 'a drinking vessel (we hope)'. Mister = the Reed Blowpipe, a fine spray for delicate work.
arenas: Close Quarters: The Crawlway, single file only.
King of the Hill: The Ceiling Chamber, the most-photographed wall in prehistory.
Turbulence: The Cave Mouth, where winter wind blows paint back in your face.
Movement Course: The Descent, a route of ledges that 'probably had ritual significance'.
The Hall of Beasts: a famous gallery, now with two bands fighting over the beasts.
Gift Shop: the same cave in the present day, with the rope barriers as platforms.
premises.tone: Prehistoric slapstick narrated by a pompous museum. The joke is the gap between a brutal paint brawl and the reverent placard written about it. Captions: 'ritual site (probably)' / 'cloud (pictured: cloud. we think. do not move)' / 'by grunk (age 7, est.)'.
premises.art_fit: Excellent. Cave painting is the world's original crude art, so stick figures, wobbly outlines and blobby fills are period-accurate. Light-grey doodles become older, fainter paintings. The canvas can stay white with a caption: 'wall (cleaned by archaeologists)'.
premises.risks: Cavemen are well-worn comedy and need the museum double timeline to feel fresh. It is ancient-past whimsy rather than cosmic weirdness. Caves invite dark levels, so keep the darkness to the torch reveal only.

coherence.reason: Cave painting is the original crude art and the museum's double timeline gives a great reason the score comes 40,000 years late, but cavemen are well-worn comedy and it is whimsy rather than strangeness.

identity.reason: Cave painting is the original crude art and the confidently wrong museum placards are funny, but caveman comedy is well-worn and has less weird confidence than the leaders.

production.reason: Cave painting is the original crude art, and the confidently wrong museum placards ('by grunk (age 7, est.)') are a great caption engine, but cavemen are well-worn and caves pull toward darkness.

premises.name: The Ministry of Approved Colours
premises.logline: Colour has been rationed since the war and nobody ever repealed it. The only way a department gets a bigger ration next quarter is to have more of its colour on the walls when the Surveyor comes round.
premises.world: A drab, cheerful bureaucratic nation where white and grey are free and everything else needs a coupon. Pigment is issued by the Ministry of Approved Colours, on forms, to licensed officers only. Yellow is so scarce that the sun was issued in grey. Each quarter's ration is shared in proportion to the national surface already in each department's colour, so departments send officers out to apply it. The system feeds itself, and nobody has ever questioned it.
premises.who_you_play: Grade 7 Colour Officers, licensed to carry and apply pigment, in regulation overalls and Form CP-3 headwear (the flat cap). The box head is regulation too: Schedule 2 requires personnel to be fileable. Faces are two dots and a line because expressions need a separate licence.
premises.why_paint: Coverage is next quarter's ration, and the ration is power. Counting colour without a Surveyor's licence is an offence, so nobody on the ground knows the score. The reveal is the Quarterly Survey: a Surveyor with a clipboard walks the site stamping each slab, and the result is printed in the Gazette under a headline that is always phrased as boringly as possible.
premises.teams: Two rival departments with real grudges: the Department of Ceilings (aloof and looks down on everyone) against the Office of Floors (Provisional), which has been provisional since 1952 and is bitter about it. Colours are random because the Ministry assigns them by lottery from Schedule 4, 'Approved Pairings', to prevent favouritism.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = 'Dispersal Unit (Form D)'. Roller = 'Flat Application Device, Standard'. Bucket = 'Bulk Requisition', issued only in triplicate. Mister = 'Atmospheric Allocation (approval pending)'. Later: the Rubber Stamp (melee, leaves a seal) and the Red Tape (a barrier).
arenas: Close Quarters: Room 4B (Overflow). The waiting room, with the queue still in it.
King of the Hill: The Ministry Steps. Paint the top step for a paperwork advantage.
Turbulence: The Directorate of Air Vents. Air is rationed too, badly.
Movement Course: Fitness for Duty Assessment. Mandatory, annual, and nobody passes.
The Archive: filing cabinets as platforms, with drawers labelled 'GREY (MISC)'.
The Coupon Exchange: a trading floor whose only commodity is a teaspoon of red.
premises.tone: Warm civil-service Kafka. Rubber stamps, cheerful forms, total obedience. Nobody is oppressed; they are just processed. Captions: 'SUN (YELLOW IS RATIONED)' / 'THIS CLOUD HAS NOT BEEN APPROVED' / 'PLEASE TAKE A NUMBER (numbers are grey)'.
premises.art_fit: It gives the best legal reason for 'team hues never appear in the world': outside a sanctioned job they are contraband. The white and grey world is the free tier. Crude lines are the Ministry draughtsmen working on government-surplus PCs, and the existing 'YELLOW IS TAKEN' joke becomes law.
premises.risks: Rationing and bureaucracy can drift into grim dystopia, so it must stay jolly and paper-based. It is text-heavy and depends on the forms being funny. It overlaps Planning Permission and Kerb Appeal in civic-deadpan register.

coherence.reason: Rationing gives a watertight legal reason why team hues never appear and turns the existing 'YELLOW IS TAKEN' joke into law, but it leans on text and drifts toward dystopia.

identity.reason: It gives the best legal reason why team hues are absent ('SUN (YELLOW IS RATIONED)'), but it is text-heavy civil-service Kafka with a narrow appeal and overlaps the other civic premises.

production.reason: It gives the best legal reason why team hues never appear in the world, and the Ceilings versus Floors (Provisional) feud is great, but it is text-heavy and repeats the civic deadpan of two other premises.

premises.name: Hold Still
premises.logline: By law, a town is whatever colour its official photograph says, and the photograph is taken once a century. The last one was black and white. The photographer is back with two-colour film, and he keeps asking for another take.
premises.world: Burnham-on-Grey was photographed in 1926 in black and white, so for a hundred years it has been grey by statute. Now the Official Photographer has returned with two-strip colour film, which can only capture two colours. Two rival guilds of decorators get the length of one exposure to paint the town before the shutter closes. He is never happy with the shot, so every match is announced as the next take: 'TAKE 14'.
premises.who_you_play: Guild decorators who have been posing since 1926. The box-head flat-cap figure is a 1920s working man exactly as he appeared in the original photograph: squared up, still, cap on and expression flat, because you did not smile in photos then. Overalls in guild colours are a fresh scandal in a town that has never had colour.
premises.why_paint: Whatever colour is in the photograph is legally the town's colour for the next century. The winning guild gets the hundred-year maintenance contract and its colour on every postcard. The photograph has not been developed, so nobody knows the score. The reveal: 'Everybody hold still', a magnesium flash, and then the print slowly developing in a tray as the count fills in.
premises.teams: Two guilds: the Worshipful Company of Rollermen against the Brush Society (Lodge 7). Colours are random because the Photographer's two-strip film only renders certain pairs, and which stock he has loaded is out of your hands. Each authored pair is a film stock: 'STOCK A: BLUE & ORANGE'.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = the Whitewash Pump (1926 Pattern). Roller = the Long Roller. Bucket = the Slop, the guilds' oldest and least dignified tool. Mister = Tint Fog, officially 'for the background'.
arenas: Close Quarters: The Coal Shed.
King of the Hill: Memorial Hill. Whoever paints the top is in the middle of the shot.
Turbulence: The Pier, In Weather.
Movement Course: The Photographer's Ladder. He needs height for the wide shot.
Town Square: the centre of the frame, where most of the photograph is.
The Darkroom: red light and drying lines, where the reveal happens.
premises.tone: A civic ceremony played completely straight, with a brass band somewhere and everyone told not to blink. Captions: 'THIS CLOUD WAS IN THE 1926 PHOTO. DO NOT MOVE IT.' / 'NOBODY BLINK' / 'SUN (NOT IN SHOT)'.
premises.art_fit: It makes the grey world the law and the absent team hues something that has never existed here. It explains the frozen deadpan faces and the cap from the original photograph. The flash-and-develop reveal is cheap: a white flash and a fill animation.
premises.risks: Once a century clashes with endless rematches, so 'TAKE N' has to be in the UI. The period setting may pull the art toward sepia pastiche, so it has to stay crude Paint. It is whimsical and the least explicitly a war.

coherence.reason: Two-strip film stock is the best explanation in the set for authored random pairs, and the town is grey by statute, but it is whimsical rather than a war, and 'TAKE N' has to carry the rematches.

identity.reason: The 1926 photograph explains the frozen deadpan faces nicely, but it is whimsical rather than a war, and a once-a-century photograph sits awkwardly with endless rematches.

production.reason: It explains the flat faces and the cap through a 1926 photograph, and 'TAKE 14' handles rematches, but it is whimsical rather than a war and invites sepia pastiche.

premises.name: Books Up
premises.logline: In the back pages of a shared rough book, two desk-mates have fought a silent war of doodles for a whole term, and the doodles have formed armies. Whoever's colour covers more of the page when the teacher says 'Books up' owns that page forever.
premises.world: The last page of a shared exercise book is a sovereign nation that adults do not know exists. Each match is one lesson. The teacher's voice is distant thunder, shown in captions ('...and if we carry the one...'), and the bell is the apocalypse. The margin doodles are a warrior culture with a deep history going back to the first page of term, and they are completely serious about it.
premises.who_you_play: The doodles. Box head, dot eyes, flat mouth and flat cap, because this is the only man either kid can draw and they draw him a hundred times a lesson. Only the overalls carry colour, because they were coloured in with felt-tip during a boring bit. The kid's name is on the cap brim in tiny capitals.
premises.why_paint: Coloured-in is ownership. A coloured patch is 'done', and done things belong to whoever coloured them. Neither side can see the score because the kids' hands are covering the page, so you only ever see your own patch. The reveal is 'BOOKS UP': the hands lift, the page is held up to the classroom window and both colours show at once, bleeding slightly through to the next page.
premises.teams: LEFT HAND and RIGHT HAND, the two desk-mates (one of them is left-handed, which comes up). Colours are random because they share one pencil case of felt-tips and most have run dry, so the teams are whichever two still work. A caption over the draw: 'the black one is for the teacher only'.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = a felt-tip flicked across the page (dot-spatter). Roller = a highlighter dragged flat, wide and translucent. Bucket = a knocked-over cup of paint water from art, played as the emergency it is. Mister = ink blown through a straw. Later: the compass point (melee), Tipp-Ex (erases to a sticky, slow white) and the rubber.
arenas: Close Quarters: the Margin. A tall, thin, red-ruled strip with no room to breathe.
King of the Hill: the Inkblot, where a pen leaked. A big black hill everyone wants.
Turbulence: the page under the classroom fan, which keeps lifting the corner.
Movement Course: a dot-to-dot, where platforms appear as the numbers are joined.
Graph Paper: the maths page, where every surface snaps to a grid.
The Spine: two pages at once, with the binding as a deep valley in the middle.
premises.tone: Hushed wartime gravity about something tiny and forbidden, like a war film whispered so the teacher won't hear. Captions: 'SILENCE IN THE MARGIN' / 'this page is supposed to be fractions' / a scrawled plaque, 'here fell Gary, rubbed out in Period 3'.
premises.art_fit: Strong. Light-grey ruled lines are free backdrop doodles, and wobbly lines are a hand working under a desk. Leaky fills are felt-tip bleed, and handwritten captions are already the house style. A 'scanned in at 72 dpi' framing keeps the aliased Paint look honest.
premises.risks: It moves the medium from screen to paper, which works against pure Paint pixels unless the page is shown as scanned. Classroom settings can feel twee. The teacher must stay unseen, a voice in captions, or it becomes a cartoon about school rather than a world.

coherence.reason: Hands covering the page is a clever reason the score is hidden and the whispered war tone is distinctive, but paper and felt-tip pull away from Paint pixels.

identity.reason: A whispered war-film tone about margin doodles is charming and relatable, and 'Books up' is a good reveal, but it moves the medium from Paint to paper.

production.reason: The whispered war-film tone is charming, but paper and felt-tip pull away from Paint pixels, and the hands covering the page is a weak reason for the hidden score.

premises.name: The Decorated Dead
premises.logline: Every decorator who ever died is still working. The afterlife is a vast blank show home under redecoration for all eternity, and when two crews disagree about the colour scheme, they settle it the only way decorators know.
premises.world: The afterlife is white because the dead lose their colour. It is an echoing, unfinished show home: dust sheets, scaffolding, grey plaster and one radio playing somewhere. Its residents are the souls of tradesmen who could not let a job go. They have a union, an eternal tea break and a client nobody has ever met. The grey backdrop doodles are ghosts of furniture nobody has decided on.
premises.who_you_play: The decorated dead. The painter tradesman is kept exactly as drawn, because the cap, the overalls and the box head are what they were wearing when they went. Their dot eyes are a little hollow and their flat mouths are permanently resigned. They are not sad; there is just work to do. Being knocked out is 'knocking off for tea', and you come back when the kettle has boiled.
premises.why_paint: Paint is memory. It is the only colour in the afterlife, and the dead make it only from what they remember. A painted surface is a remembered room made real again. The crew whose colour covers most becomes the scheme, and the scheme is what heaven looks like until the next dispute. The reveal is the snagging walk: when the shift ends, the Inspector (shown only as a clipboard and an enormous pair of shoes) walks the job, and one crew's work is signed off.
premises.teams: Every ghost remembers the last colour they ever painted, and crews are made up by lot from whoever is on shift. That is why the pairs are random. Team hues never appear in the background because nothing in the afterlife has colour of its own: 'HEAVEN (UNDER REDECORATION)'.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = the Spray Rig, a job's worth of colour in a hurry. Roller = the Roller they were buried with. Bucket = the Last Tin, thrown in one go. Mister = the Mist Coat, the thin first layer nobody ever has patience for. Later: the Ladder (weapon, platform and trip hazard) and the Dust Sheet (hides what is under it).
arenas: Close Quarters: The Airing Cupboard of the Afterlife.
King of the Hill: The Pearly Stairs. Unfinished, with one handrail missing.
Turbulence: Limbo. A draughty corridor with a window nobody has ever closed.
Movement Course: The Snagging List. Every flaw from every job ever done, built into one course.
The Waiting Room: chairs, a ticket machine and a number that is never called.
The Client's Room: locked, always. Something hums inside.
premises.tone: Gentle, dry, working-class purgatory comedy. Death is a long shift, not a tragedy. Captions: 'TEA BREAK: ETERNAL' / 'MIND THE WET PAINT (IT HAS BEEN WET SINCE 1874)' / on the results screen, 'Signed off. See you next eternity.'
premises.art_fit: It keeps every figure as drawn and makes it weird. The white canvas is the afterlife, light-grey doodles are ghost furniture, and the absence of colour is cosmology. Crude, simple ghosts suit crude art.
premises.risks: Death themes may unsettle younger players or storefronts, so it must stay gentle. The joke is quiet, so the first screen has to sell it. It overlaps The Last Coat (eternal guild, unseen client).

coherence.reason: A gentle, confident afterlife where paint is memory keeps every figure as drawn, but the death theme is a storefront risk and the joke is quiet.

identity.reason: It keeps the figure exactly as drawn and has a lovely dry tone, but the joke is quiet, the death framing carries storefront risk, and it overlaps The Last Coat.

production.reason: The gentle working-class purgatory is warm and keeps the figures, but the joke is quiet, death may worry storefronts, and it overlaps The Last Coat.

premises.name: Burn-In
premises.logline: After hours, an old office monitor runs a screensaver called 'Watching Paint Dry', and its workers know that anything left on screen long enough burns permanently into the glass. Two crews race to be the ghost that stays.
premises.world: An empty office after hours, an old CRT and the forgotten screensaver 'Watching Paint Dry', a white wall that someone is always painting. When nobody touches the mouse for five minutes, the screensaver starts and becomes a place, with grey doodled scenery and little workers who clock on when the humans clock off. Any movement of the mouse ends the world instantly. Everyone inside knows the old rule: whatever stays on screen too long burns into the phosphor and stays there forever.
premises.who_you_play: Idle Workers, the screensaver's night shift. Their box heads are low-poly by design, from a screensaver made in 1997 with the least effort possible. Flat caps are shift caps and overalls are in the crew's phosphor colour. They are not allowed to exist while anyone is watching, which gives the work an after-hours, faintly forbidden energy.
premises.why_paint: Burn-in is immortality. Colour held on a surface long enough is etched into the glass, so territory you hold outlives you and the screensaver. Burn-in is invisible while the screen is lit, so the score cannot be seen. The reveal is the monitor switching off: the picture collapses to a white dot, and in the dark glass the ghost image of whoever painted more is left faintly glowing.
premises.teams: Two phosphor crews. Colours are random because the screensaver's 'Random Colours' box has been ticked since 1997, and these are the only pairs it knows.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = the Phosphor Gun, a CRT's electron gun, sawn off. Roller = the Degausser, which warps everything it passes over. Bucket = the White Flash, the one frame where the whole screen goes bright. Mister = Static, slow channel snow that sticks.
arenas: Close Quarters: 640x480. That is all of it.
King of the Hill: The Clock, the one thing on screen that never moves, and the first to burn in.
Turbulence: Flying Pipes. A rival screensaver bleeds through and lays pipes under your feet.
Movement Course: The Bouncing Logo, which hits the exact corner once per match.
Desktop Icons: the icon grid the screensaver covers, with the Recycle Bin as a hazard.
premises.tone: Lonely, nocturnal and a little heroic: blue-collar workers on a shift nobody knows exists. Captions: 'DO NOT MOVE THE MOUSE' / 'SHIFT ENDS WHEN SOMEONE COMES BACK FROM LUNCH' / on the results screen, 'THIS WILL BE HERE LONG AFTER YOU'.
premises.art_fit: Good. 'Watching Paint Dry' keeps the white canvas and the painter look literal, crude art fits low-effort screensaver sprites, and the switch-off reveal is cheap: a white dot, a fade and a ghost layer.
premises.risks: Burn-in is fading knowledge and may need one line of explanation. 'The mouse moves and the world ends' begs for a sudden-death mechanic the game may not want. The switch-off reveal pulls the palette toward dark CRT, so keep the darkness to the reveal only.

coherence.reason: Burn-in as immortality and the switch-off reveal are evocative and cheap, but it needs explaining to anyone who never owned a CRT and invites an unwanted sudden-death rule.

identity.reason: Burn-in as immortality and the switch-off reveal are evocative, but the concept needs explaining and pulls the palette toward dark CRT.

production.reason: Burn-in as immortality is a lovely idea, but the knowledge is fading, it pulls the palette dark, and 'moving the mouse ends the world' implies a mechanic the game does not have.

premises.name: The Foreman's at Lunch
premises.logline: Under the Double Booking Act of 1911, every client hires two decorating firms for one job, and the colour that covers more of the house when the client gets back from the garden centre gets paid. Until then, nobody is allowed to measure.
premises.world: A nation whose national character is indecision. Every client books two firms, the firms settle it on site, the client's verdict is final, and by law the client must be off the premises while it happens. Decorating has become a competitive trade in the full sporting sense, with league tables, apprentice trading cards and a tea break that is sacred and enforced by statute. Radio 2 is always on.
premises.who_you_play: Journeyman decorators from rival firms. The flat cap and overalls are trade pride. The flat-topped head is a ledge for a mug of tea, and the cap keeps the mug level. Overalls are in firm colours because the Act says so, and the Act is never wrong.
premises.why_paint: Coverage is the invoice. The client pays by the square metre for the colour they end up with, and they end up with whichever there is more of. Section 4 of the Act makes it an offence to measure a job before the client has inspected it, so there is no running score. The reveal is the client in the doorway, holding a potted plant, squinting, and saying 'I think I like the...' while a tape measure unspools across the floor.
premises.teams: Two firms, for example 'Harding & Sons' against 'Brush Bros (Est. Tuesday)'. Colours are random because the client chose the shortlist, not you: each authored pair is a swatch card the client brought home from the shop, always two colours, never decided.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = 'the Airless'. Old hands consider it cheating, and it is legal. Roller = 'the Nine-Inch', the trade's honest tool. Bucket = 'the Slosh', banned on commercial jobs since 1911, but the Act forgot about private homes. Mister = 'the Touch-Up Atomiser', for a fine finish, it says on the box. Later: the Ladder (weapon, platform and trip hazard) and the Dust Sheet (hides what is under it).
arenas: Close Quarters: The Downstairs Loo. Two firms, one en-suite, no room to swing a roller.
King of the Hill: The Loft Conversion. Whoever holds the apex holds the quote.
Turbulence: The Conservatory, Gale Force 8. The client left a window open, as clients do.
Movement Course: The Apprentice Assessment Rig. Pass it and you get your cap.
Scaffold: a job that is all planks and ladders, with Health & Safety absent.
The Garden Centre: away fixture. The client is here, so no painting near the client.
premises.tone: Builder's-yard deadpan: weary professionals taking a ridiculous system completely seriously. Captions: 'CLIENT AT GARDEN CENTRE (BACK SOON)' / 'MIND THE DUST SHEETS (there are no dust sheets)' / 'QUOTE VALID 30 DAYS OR UNTIL SOMEONE WINS'.
premises.art_fit: It needs the fewest changes to the existing art. The house is in undercoat, primed white and grey because nobody has chosen a colour yet, which is why team hues never appear. Crude arenas read as the foreman's quote sketch on the back of an invoice.
premises.risks: It is the closest to the current implicit theme, so it is the safest and least weird. All of the weirdness rests on the Double Booking Act, so the Act has to be on screen early and often. The client is offstage, so the reveal has to carry the character.

coherence.reason: The Double Booking Act explains everything tidily and needs the fewest art changes, but it is the least weird premise and depends on the Act being on screen constantly.

identity.reason: It is the safest fit with the current tradesman theme and the Double Booking Act is a decent joke, but it is the least weird premise and essentially the status quo with lore added.

production.reason: The Double Booking Act is a funny, confident hook that changes almost no art, but it is barely weirder than the current implicit theme.

premises.name: Two Colours Out of Space
premises.logline: The universe was grey until two colours arrived on the same meteor, rival strains from outside space-time, each cheerfully colonising Earth. You are one of their hosts. Your head went square when it moved in, and it is very happy with you.
premises.world: Physics only provides light and shade, so the universe is naturally grey. Colour is an organism from outside space-time, and two rival strains landed on the same meteor. Neither is malicious; both are extremely expansionist and a little smug. Each strain lives in surfaces and uses humans for transport, because humans have hands, can jump and will do anything if it is phrased as a sport.
premises.who_you_play: Hosts. When the colour moves in, it remodels you for efficiency. The head goes square, because the colour likes right angles (they pack better). The face simplifies to two dots and a line. You grow a flat cap, which is a lid to keep the colour in. Your overalls are not clothing; they are the colour showing through. One caption describes a host as 'previously Dave'.
premises.why_paint: Painted surface is literally colonised territory: wherever the colour spreads, it is alive. Coverage decides which strain gets the planet. The score is hidden because only colour can perceive colour, and hosts are too grey inside to tell. The reveal is a slow zoom out to a telescope in a far-off grey civilisation, where an astronomer squints at Earth and writes down what colour it is now.
premises.teams: The two strains. The pairs are random because each meteor carries a different pair, and pairs are the colour's mating types, fixed by its biology. No other combination can share a rock.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = a spore pump grown from the host's arm, drawn as a sprayer because that is what the colour thinks a sprayer is. Roller = the Spreading Organ, a cylindrical growth best rolled along floors. Bucket = the Bloom, a whole culture flung in one burst. Mister = the Exhale, which hosts do not like to talk about.
arenas: Close Quarters: The Impact Crater, still warm.
King of the Hill: The Observatory, the highest point and the first place that will be seen.
Turbulence: The Upper Atmosphere, where spores fight jet streams.
Movement Course: The Quarantine Zone. Hazard-tape platforms built by people who gave up.
Grey Suburb: an uncolonised street where the neighbours are visibly worried.
The Meteor: inside the original rock, where both strains came from.
premises.tone: Cheerful cosmic horror, narrated by the colour in an upbeat corporate voice, delighted with its hosts and politely unaware anything is wrong. Captions: 'humanity (former, thriving)' / 'this cloud has not joined us yet. it will' / 'grey (sad, temporary)'.
premises.art_fit: Strong. The box head is biology, and the crude style is what an alien colour thinks people look like. The grey world against colour is the whole fiction: everything not yet colonised is grey. Leaky fills are colour spreading like an organism.
premises.risks: Its 'paint is the body' logic rhymes with Splatoon even though nothing is a sea creature or ink, so the possession framing has to keep it distinct. Possession and body horror may skew darker than the author's deadpan, so the chirpy narrator must carry it. It also echoes a famous Lovecraft title, so the on-screen name may want changing.

coherence.reason: Colonising colour explains the box heads and the grey world with a chirpy horror tone, but paint-as-body sits close to Splatoon's ink biology, and possession skews dark.

identity.reason: 'Previously Dave' is funny, but the 'colour is your body' logic rhymes too closely with Splatoon's ink biology, and the title borrows from Lovecraft.

production.reason: The chirpy alien narrator is fun, but a colour living in the body rhymes with Splatoon's biology, and the body-horror pull fights the deadpan tone.

premises.name: The Final Inspection
premises.logline: The apocalypse came as a fresh coat of landlord magnolia. Colour survives only in the last tins in the last sheds, and when the Landlord descends from the sky to inspect the property, tenants keep whatever they have improved.
premises.world: One morning the sky, the sea and the grass were all 'neutralised for resale'. This was the Beigening. Above the world stands the Landlord, a vast, patient entity with a clipboard who owns everything and returns now and then to inspect it. Under the old tenancy agreement the Landlord honours the Bond: any surface a tenant has improved is theirs. So the tenants improve, violently.
premises.who_you_play: Post-apocalyptic decorators: the painter tradesman played completely straight in the worst economy there has ever been. Flat caps, overalls and box heads are Guild of Tenants issue. A regulation head means the Landlord cannot tell anyone apart and evict them individually. Getting knocked out is 'served notice', and you are back in after the usual 30 seconds.
premises.why_paint: Paint is the only property left. A painted surface is an improvement, an improvement is equity, and equity is survival. Nobody knows what the Landlord thinks until the inspection, so there is no running score. The reveal is a huge clipboard lowering into frame, a tick against every square metre, and then a stamp over each team: BOND RETURNED or BOND WITHHELD.
premises.teams: Two rival tenant cooperatives in the same block. Colours are random because they use whatever tins they found in the shed that morning, and the authored pairs are the only matching sets left on earth. A pre-match caption: 'today's tins: PINK and GREEN (no returns)'.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = a pump sprayer jury-rigged from a bike pump and a fire extinguisher. Roller = a decorator's roller on a broom handle, a family heirloom. Bucket = the last tin, thrown whole, which tenants call 'the deposit'. Mister = a plant mister from before the Beigening, still smelling faintly of ferns.
arenas: Close Quarters: a box room the Landlord lists as a 'double bedroom'.
King of the Hill: the communal stairwell, whose top landing is inspected first.
Turbulence: the bit of the property above the boiler, where the air does things.
Movement Course: scaffolding left up since 2009, 'pending works'.
The Garden: a grey lawn with a sign reading NO BALL GAMES, NO PAINT GAMES.
Magnolia Mile: a corridor so beige it has its own weather.
premises.tone: British rental misery at the end of the world: kitchen-sink realism, bleak, resigned and quietly heroic. Captions: 'NO NAILS IN WALLS (or anywhere)' / 'landlord's cloud: do not move, do not paint, do not look at' / 'damp (structural, beloved)'.
premises.art_fit: The white canvas is the magnolia that covers everything, and a caption insists it is beige. Grey slabs are unimproved property. Crude drawing is all a tenant is permitted, because good artwork would count as a fixture and the Landlord would keep it.
premises.risks: It is close to the current tradesman theme and could read as a reskin, not the leap the author wants. The landlord satire is UK-flavoured and can turn genuinely bitter if the jokes stop being absurd. It shares a 'cosmic client with a clipboard' with The Last Coat and The Decorated Dead, so pick one.

coherence.reason: The Beigening and the Bond explain coverage and the white world well, but it is close to a reskin of the tradesmen and its landlord satire can turn bitter.

identity.reason: 'The Beigening' is a good word, but rental misery skews bitter, and the premise reads as a reskin of the tradesman theme.

production.reason: The Beigening is a good gag, but this is mostly a reskin of the tradesman theme with a bleaker rental-misery tone that could turn sour after 100 matches.

premises.name: Recovered (1) and (2)
premises.logline: A hard drive died, and two damaged copies of the same picture were recovered into the same sectors. Only one can be the real file, and the copy that fills more of the disk keeps the name.
premises.world: The inside of a file-recovery wizard, mid-progress bar. The picture was a crew of painters, saved as ColourWars.bmp. Two copies survived, 'ColourWars (1).bmp' and 'ColourWars (2).bmp', and they have been written over the same stretch of disk. Same picture, same arenas, same people, but each copy's palette header was corrupted differently, so they disagree about what colour everything is.
premises.who_you_play: The same box-head painter, twice. The picture was of a decorating crew, and both copies have the whole crew, so every player is fighting their own duplicate. That explains identical models across teams better than any costume could. Each copy is completely sure it is the original.
premises.why_paint: The recovery tool keeps whichever version holds the most sectors, and every painted surface is a sector claimed for your copy. The disk is read in order and nothing is counted until the scan finishes, so nobody can tell who is ahead. The reveal is the recovery report scrolling in: 'RECOVERED: ColourWars (2).bmp - 61%. (1) WAS DISCARDED.'
premises.teams: Copy (1) and Copy (2). The random colour pairs are the corruption itself: each recovery damages the palette headers differently, so every match the copies come back with a new disagreement (blue against orange, pink against green).
premises.weapons: Sprayer = Bit Scatter, which sprays bytes. Roller = Sector Overwrite, one straight run. Bucket = Cluster Dump, a whole block at once that may land anywhere. Mister = Bit Rot, slow and patient and everywhere. Glitch stripes and misaligned rows are hand-drawn and crude.
arenas: Close Quarters: The File Header. The cramped first 54 bytes.
King of the Hill: The Bad Sector, the one spot both copies need and nothing can be written to.
Turbulence: Spin-Up. The disk is still turning, and the arena scrolls by row as it is read.
Movement Course: The Defragmenter. Blocks shuffle around under your feet.
Thumbs.db: a tiny cached thumbnail of the whole picture, which is out of date.
premises.tone: Deadpan existential slapstick: two identical idiots, each sure they are the original. Captions: 'YOU ARE THE ORIGINAL. (SO ARE THEY.)' / 'DO NOT RENAME THIS FILE' / '0 BYTES WERE HARMED. 4,096 WERE OVERWRITTEN.'
premises.art_fit: Good. A glitched bitmap forgives everything, and crude art plus hand-drawn corruption stripes is very cheap. It does pull the clean white canvas toward glitch art, so keep the glitches sparse and drawn, never generated.
premises.risks: File-system jargon can turn into exposition. 'Fight your double' is a strong hook, but the teams have no identity beyond their copy number. It is the third 'inside a computer' premise, so it competes with Save Changes and Burn-In.

coherence.reason: Fighting your own duplicate explains the identical models brilliantly, but the teams have no identity beyond a copy number and file-system jargon creeps in.

identity.reason: 'Fight your own duplicate' neatly explains why both teams use the same model, but the teams have no identity of their own and file-system jargon tends toward exposition.

production.reason: Fighting your own corrupted duplicate neatly explains identical models, but the teams have no identity and the file-system jargon wears thin quickly.

premises.name: Teatime Rules
premises.logline: On a wet Saturday two siblings invent a game called 'Painters', and its cardboard pieces treat the rules as the laws of physics, even though the rules change every five minutes. The match ends when someone shouts 'TEA'S READY'.
premises.world: The world is the inside of a made-up game in a living room: cushions, chairs and an empty paint tray. The rules are written in felt-tip on a scrap of cardboard taped to the wall, numbered and contradictory, and the figures obey them with total solemnity. 'RULE 9: the floor is lava. RULE 9b: not YOUR colour of floor.' New rules appear in captions mid-match, in a child's handwriting.
premises.who_you_play: The game pieces: cardboard men the kids drew and cut out. Box heads because circles are hard with blunt scissors, flat caps because Dad's a decorator and the game is called 'Painters'. Each kid coloured their own team's overalls.
premises.why_paint: Rule 1 is 'whoever paints the most floor wins', and in this world rules are physics. Unpainted floor is lava; your colour is safe ground. Nobody counts during the game because counting is boring and you do it at the end (Rule 3). The reveal is 'TEA'S READY!' from the kitchen. The game freezes and the two kids count it out loud in a hurried, increasingly argumentative tally that ticks up on screen, until a grown-up voice settles it.
premises.teams: Two siblings, both of whom will claim to have won. Colours are random because every round starts with both kids grabbing a felt-tip from the mug without looking (Rule 5). Swapping is banned by Rule 4: 'NO SWAPSIES'.
