premises.weapons: Sprayer = 'the Squirter', a squeezy washing-up bottle. Roller = Dad's actual roller, which nobody is allowed to touch (Rule 6). Bucket = the paint tray, tipped over. Mister = Mum's plant mister. Later: the Pillow Bomb (knockback), Base (a respawn zone nobody can paint) and BACKSIES (undoes the last three seconds of your own paint, once a game).
arenas: Close Quarters: Under the Dining Table. Very cramped, chair legs everywhere.
King of the Hill: the Sofa Cushion Pile.
Turbulence: the Radiator Window, where hot air lifts you.
Movement Course: the Stairs, which are banned (Rule 2), so the whole course is stair-sliding.
The Hallway: a long thin stage with the front door as a gust trap.
The Bath: no water, just a slippery tub and a lot of shower-curtain cover.
premises.tone: Breathless rule-lawyering childhood logic, met with absolute sincerity by the pieces. Captions: 'RULE 14: the cushions are a mountain' / 'RULE 15: ok the cushions are ALSO lava' / on the results screen, 'BOTH WON (said Mum)'.
premises.art_fit: Good. Cardboard cut-outs and a felt-tip rule sign suit crude drawing. Numbered rules give the deadpan captions a natural home, and furniture becomes grey slab silhouettes. It is 'crude because a kid made it' rather than literally Paint.exe, which still justifies every wobble.
premises.risks: Rules that change in captions could make players expect real rule changes, so keep it to captions or a small set of match modifiers. A living room is less weird than the brief wants, so the weirdness has to come from rules-as-physics. A pure tie reveal ('BOTH WON') must never replace the real result.

coherence.reason: Rules as physics is charming, but a living room is not weird enough, and captioned rule changes set false expectations of real ones.

identity.reason: Rules-as-physics captions are fun, but a living-room game of make-believe is not weird enough and risks confusion with real rule changes.

production.reason: Numbered felt-tip rules make a great home for captions, but a living room is mild, and caption-only rule changes would confuse players who expect real modifiers.

premises.name: Before Morning
premises.logline: Every night two boxed sets of 'My First Decorator' peg dolls redecorate a child's bedroom, because tomorrow the child will play with whichever toys' colour they wake up to. The losers go back in the toybox.
premises.world: A child's bedroom after lights-out. Only one kind of toy matters: the peg dolls from two knock-off 'My First Decorator' playsets, with flat caps, overalls, tiny sprayers, rollers and buckets. They know the one law of the bedroom: in the morning the child opens their eyes, sees the room, and plays all day with whichever toys' colour is everywhere. These toys were made to decorate and think of themselves as tradesmen, so they fight like rival firms over a contract that renews every night.
premises.who_you_play: Junior Decorator peg dolls, which keeps the box head, dot eyes, flat cap and team overalls exactly as drawn. The crude face is cheap factory printing: two dots and a line, slightly off. This is the most faithful tradesman premise in the set, moved into toy life.
premises.why_paint: Coverage is your future. The toys that get played with are loved, and unplayed toys gather dust in the box. Nobody can see the whole room in the dark, so the score is unknowable until the curtains open. The reveal is dawn: the alarm goes off, the curtains are pulled and sunlight sweeps across the floor, revealing coverage strip by strip, with a sleepy child-voice caption: 'woah'.
premises.teams: Two rival playset brands, knock-offs of each other, bought on two different birthdays. Colours are random because the cheap factory packed the paint pots at random. The box admits it: 'colours may vary'.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = the playset's squeeze-bulb spray gun. Roller = the toy roller, the playset's pride. Bucket = the toy bucket. Mister = a toy watering can. Later: the Wind-Up Van (transport), the Stamp Set (a placeable paint stamp) and the Night Light (a turret, and painted areas near it glow at dawn).
arenas: Close Quarters: Under the Bed. Cramped and full of lost socks.
King of the Hill: the Top Bunk.
Turbulence: the Open Window, with the curtain flapping.
Movement Course: a marble run built across the shelves.
The Toybox: where the losers sleep, a deep dark respawn arena.
The Dolls' House: a whole small house inside the room, which also needs redecorating.
premises.tone: A quiet midnight caper with tradesman professionalism, warm and slightly melancholy. Captions: 'NO JOB TOO SMALL (all jobs are small)' / 'this teddy has seen everything' / 'colours may vary. Ages 3+. Not suitable for walls.'
premises.art_fit: Good. Peg dolls justify the box heads and the crude printed faces. To keep the Paint.exe look honest, the bedroom should be the child's own drawing of the bedroom. The dawn reveal is a lighting sweep, a cheap theatrical ending.
premises.risks: 'Toys live at night' sits close to Toy Story, so the trade pride and the colour-judging child must dominate. A night lighting pass may cost more than a solo budget wants, so it is better to imply darkness with a grey wash. It is the safest premise in the set, a strength for the tradesman preference and a weakness against 'weird like Splatoon'.

coherence.reason: The most faithful tradesman premise with a nice dawn reveal, but it sits close to Toy Story and is the safest, least weird option.

identity.reason: It is a faithful tradesman premise, but it sits too close to Toy Story and is the least weird in the set.

production.reason: It is the most faithful to the tradesman look but the least weird, it reads close to Toy Story, and night lighting costs art time.

premises.name: Low Ink
premises.logline: The world is a page stuck in a printer queue, and one of its two colour cartridges has been flagged as nearly empty. Each must prove it still has ink by putting more of itself on the page before the print comes out, because the flagged one goes in the bin.
premises.world: An office inkjet and the job stuck in its queue: one page, shown in greyscale Print Preview. Everyone in this world is a printer driver's idea of a person. They know the printer's cruelty: one cartridge has been flagged LOW INK, nobody knows which, and the flagged one is replaced at the weekend. Cartridges are said to have souls, and they are definitely full of something.
premises.who_you_play: Cartridge crews. Each crew is the ink inside one cartridge, drawn as box-head workers because the printer's test-page figure has a box head. The flat caps and overalls are the cartridge's label livery. They are painter tradesmen in effect, decorating the one page they will ever get.
premises.why_paint: Coverage is evidence: ink on the page proves the cartridge is not empty, and the cartridge that puts down less goes in the bin. The preview is greyscale, so the score is unknowable mid-match. The reveal is the print itself: the printer whirrs, and the finished page slides out line by line, in colour for the first and only time.
premises.teams: Two colour cartridges. The pairs are random because nobody buys the same brand twice, so whoever the shop had (blue/orange, pink/green) is who turns up.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = the Print Head, firing its nozzles. Roller = the Feed Roller, which leaves a stripe when it slips. Bucket = the Leak, the classic dropped-cartridge smear. Mister = Draft Mode: thin, fast and faint.
arenas: Close Quarters: The Margins, the slim strips the printer refuses to print on.
King of the Hill: The Paper Jam, a crumpled page raised in the middle of the arena.
Turbulence: The Feed. The page is going through, so the floor slides.
Movement Course: The Test Page, all alignment lines and calibration blocks.
Envelope: an arena printed sideways, wrong in exactly the way envelopes always are.
premises.tone: Office-drudgery satire, a fight for survival inside a beige plastic box. Captions: 'LOW INK (ONE OF YOU)' / 'PC LOAD LETTER (WE DON'T KNOW EITHER)' / on the results screen, 'THE OTHER ONE HAS BEEN SENT FOR RECYCLING'.
premises.art_fit: Good. The greyscale preview explains why team hues are absent until the reveal, and the print-out reveal is a cheap scroll of the final image. Ink smears suit leaky fills. It is about paper and ink rather than Paint.exe itself.
premises.risks: Printer misery is a universal joke but a narrow one, and it may run out after a handful of captions. The roller and bucket identities are stretched. The 'binned' framing could read as bleak. The print reveal overlaps Planning Permission's dot-matrix reveal.

coherence.reason: A greyscale preview hiding the score is neat, but printer misery is a narrow joke and the roller and bucket identities are stretched.

identity.reason: The greyscale print preview is a clever explanation of why team hues are absent, but printer jokes are narrow and the roller and bucket identities are stretched.

production.reason: The greyscale preview and print reveal work, but printer misery is a narrow joke that runs out quickly and the weapon identities are stretched.

premises.name: Culture
premises.logline: Under the lid of a forgotten Petri dish, two great mould civilisations wage the only war that counts, the war for agar, and when the experiment ends the Lab Tech lifts the lid to count the colonies.
premises.world: In an abandoned lab fridge, an entire civilisation lives on a sterile white plate of agar. To the mould it is a continent, and every match lasts three generations. They have cities, a church and opinions. The agar is land, the lid is the sky, and God is a technician with a clipboard who visits on Thursdays.
premises.who_you_play: Spore-folk, exactly as the Lab Tech draws them in the margin of his lab notebook: a box for the spore case, two dots, a line, and a flat cap that is the colony's fruiting cap. The overalls are the colony's colour. Every player is a doodle in a scientist's log, which is why they look like this. They are small, brave and deeply unhygienic.
premises.why_paint: Paint is the colony. A coloured surface has been grown on, eaten and settled, so coverage is literally population. It cannot be counted during play because mould does not stop growing to be counted. The reveal is the end of the experiment: the lid comes off, the tech squints, ticks a clipboard and declares which culture 'dominated the sample'. The other is filed as 'contamination'.
premises.teams: Each experiment, the lab swabs two random surfaces (a doorknob, a sandwich, someone's phone), so the cultures and their colours are drawn at random. Pink, green, blue and orange are all real mould colours, and the tech notes each as 'interesting'. Team hues never appear in the scenery because the agar is sterile.
premises.weapons: Sprayer = Spore Burst. Roller = the Creep, a slow fuzzy carpet. Bucket = the Bloom, one enormous wet growth. Mister = Damp, a humid fog that makes everything grow. Later: the Antibiotic Disc (a dangerous ring that kills everything near it) and the Cotton Swab.
arenas: Close Quarters: Sample 7B. A tiny dish labelled 'DO NOT OPEN'.
King of the Hill: The Crust, the highest point on a slice of bread.
Turbulence: The Fume Hood. Extraction fans blow spores everywhere.
Movement Course: The Yoghurt. Undated, ancient, sacred.
The Cheese: holes as tunnels and caves.
Behind the Fridge: a forgotten frontier of crumbs.
premises.tone: Grimy and cheerful: a solemn lab log kept by a civilisation that takes itself very seriously. Captions: 'DAY 3. DO NOT EAT.' / 'THE LID (DO NOT PRAY TO IT)' / on the loss screen, 'Your culture has been classified: CONTAMINATION.'
premises.art_fit: Good. Sterile white agar is the white canvas, mould is naturally blobby and fuzzy, which suits aliased fills and leaky buckets, and lab labels are naturally deadpan. 'Drawn by the tech in the margin' makes crude figures canon.
premises.risks: Mould is gross, and some players and storefront art will be put off, so keep everything cartoon-clean and never photographic. The joke range may run dry sooner than others. It shares 'colonising organism' with Two Colours Out of Space. The box heads need the notebook framing, or they read as forced.

coherence.reason: Mould coverage really is population, but it is gross, the notebook framing for the box heads is forced, and the jokes may run dry.

identity.reason: Mould civilisations are original, but they are gross on a storefront, and the box head needs a forced notebook framing.

production.reason: Agar as the white canvas is neat, but mould is off-putting, the joke range is narrow, and the box heads need an extra framing to justify them.

notes.coherence:
I scored 23 premises, and they sort into three groups.

**Patterns**
- **The best scorers make the existing art true inside the world.** Save Changes, Feed the Hues and Kerb Appeal don't apologise for the crude look; they make it physics, piety or anatomy.
- **The random colour pairs are the weakest link in almost every premise.** Most fall back on "a swatch card / lottery / Schedule 4". Three explain the pairs with a real mechanism instead: Hold Still (two-strip film stock), Swatch (the Ritual of the Fan) and Save Changes (Edit Colors offers candidates in pairs).
- **The end reveal is well solved across the board.** The cheapest strong reveals are the Save dialog, the Big Bang one-colour fill, Dust Sheets Off and the magnesium flash.
- **The tradesman premises cluster, and so do the computer premises.** Foreman's at Lunch, Final Inspection, Before Morning and Decorated Dead are safe but not weird; Last Coat is the one that keeps the tradesmen and becomes Splatoon-weird. Save Changes, Desktop Background, Planning Permission, Recovered, Burn-In and Low Ink all compete for one slot, and Save Changes wins it.
- **Kerb Appeal is the closest match to Splatoon's actual move.** It is a new dominant species whose bodies are the existing sprites, delivered deadpan.

**Best hybrids**
1. **Save Changes + Feed the Hues.** Keep the unsaved 16-colour file and its single free slot, so the Save stays the reveal. Make the two candidate colours petty, starving gods worshipped by Left Click and Right Click, and make THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL the first commandment. That gives a cast of characters and an escalating theology to Save Changes, which on its own risks being one joke, and gives the gods a concrete prize and reveal.
2. **The Last Coat + Save Changes**, for the user's openness to painter tradesmen. The Decorators of the End are contracted to paint the next universe, the universe is untitled.bmp, and the Big Bang is the Hand clicking Save: "UNIVERSE #4,118,002: mostly orange". This keeps the flat-cap tradesmen exactly as drawn, makes them cosmic and weird, and keeps the Paint art as literal truth.

**Reasons to borrow from other premises**
- Hold Still's film-stock idea is a reason for the colour pairs that the hybrids could adopt.
- Kerb Appeal is the strongest standalone alternative if the author wants a species premise rather than a meta one.
notes.identity:
Patterns:
(1) The strongest premises make the grey world and the absent team hues a law of the fiction rather than a style choice: the palette slot (Save Changes), extinct colour (Hue Season), starving gods (Feed the Hues), rationing (Ministry). That is the Splatoon lesson applied properly: the fiction explains the art direction, not only the mechanic.
(2) Premises that make crude drawing in-world truth score highest on art fit: Save Changes (the Hand), Feed the Hues ('THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL'), Desktop Background ('by matt (age 7)'), Cave Wall.
(3) Pure tradesman premises (Foreman's at Lunch, Before Morning, Final Inspection) are safe but fail the 'weird like Splatoon' brief. The best tradesman-preserving options make the trade cosmic or alien: The Last Coat, Hueherds.
(4) There are three clusters, and only one should be picked from each: 'inside a computer' (Save Changes, Burn-In, Recovered, Low Ink, Desktop Background); 'eternal guild and absent client' (Last Coat, Decorated Dead, Final Inspection); 'living colour' (Hue Season, Feed the Hues, Colours Out of Space, Culture, Swatch).
(5) Several reveals are cheap and strong: the Save dialog with a dither to grey, the Big Bang one-colour sky, sunset roosting, and the giant eye slurping its colour.

Best hybrid: Save Changes x Feed the Hues. Each team is a colour candidate (a hungry minor god) competing for the last palette slot, the Hand is the indifferent creator, and 'THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL' is scripture inside the file. The hybrid keeps Save Changes' one-line pitch and perfect Save-dialog reveal, adds Feed the Hues' theology and personality to the colours so the premise is not one joke, and avoids real-religion risk because the gods are palette entries. The box-head flat-cap figures stay as 'the only person the Hand can draw'. A close runner-up is The Last Coat with Hue Season's ecology, if the author wants to keep the tradesman figure: cosmic decorators herding the last living colour into the next universe.

Patterns:
1. The strongest premises make the crude art true inside the world, not just tolerated: Save Changes (aliasing is physics), Feed the Hues (drawing badly is piety), Cave Wall (period-accurate), Kerb Appeal (the box head is a house). This is criterion 4 and it separates the top tier.
2. The most common winning trick is a reason why the world is grey and team hues are scarce. Palette slots, rationing, extinction, covenant and starving gods all turn the art rule 'team hues never appear in the world' into lore. Premises without one (Before Morning, Teatime Rules, Low Ink) feel thinner.
3. The reveal is easy, and almost every premise has a decent one. The differentiator is whether the reveal also explains the rematch: the program forgets the palette, the next universe, TAKE N, the election runs again.
4. Three clusters overlap, and the author should pick one from each at most:
   - inside-a-computer: Save Changes, Desktop Background, Burn-In, Recovered, Low Ink;
   - civic deadpan: Planning Permission, Ministry, Kerb Appeal, Foreman;
   - eternal guild with an unseen client: Last Coat, Decorated Dead, Final Inspection.
5. Tradesman-faithful premises (Foreman, Before Morning, Final Inspection) score lower on weirdness. The best way to keep the overalls and still be weird is to keep the costume and change what is wearing it: houses, paint chips, Hueherds, acolytes.

Best hybrid: Save Changes + Feed the Hues.
- The world is untitled.bmp with one palette slot left, and the candidate colours are petty gods campaigning for that slot.
- The Hand's drawings are their congregations, and THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL is the Hand's own first commandment.
- Greys are dead or failed gods, which gives Taupe a gravestone in the backdrop.
- The reveal is the Save dialog, followed by the winning god filling slot 16.
- This keeps Save Changes' perfect art fit and reveal, and fixes its one-joke risk with Feed the Hues' cast of characterful colour gods, which can keep generating jokes.

Runner-up hybrid, if the author wants to keep the tradesmen: Swatch + Last Coat. Shade-named decorators choose the base coat of the next universe ('UNIVERSE #4,118,003: Burnt Mandarin'). Kerb Appeal is the strongest standalone premise outside the computer frame.
